4 Experiment

---SETUP---

4.1 Dataset

We used regression datasets with two types of covariate shift, i.e., domain shift and image corruption.

SVHN-MNIST. SVHN [44] and MNIST [36] are famous digit-recognition datasets. Although they are mainly used for classification, we used them for regression by training models to directly output a scalar value of the label. We used SVHN and MNIST as the source and target domains, respectively.

UTKFace [59]. UTKFace is a dataset consisting of face images. The task is to predict the age of the person in an input image. For the source model, we trained models on the original UTKFace images. For the target domain, we added corruptions such as noise or blur to the images. The types of corruption were the same as those of ImageNet-C [25]. We applied 13 types of corruption at the highest severity level of the five levels.

Biwi Kinect [18]. Biwi Kinect is a dataset consisting of person images. The task is to predict the head pose of the person in an input image in terms of pitch, yaw, and roll angles. We separately trained models to predict each angle. The source and target domains are the gender of the person in the image. We conducted experiments on six combinations of the source/target gender and task, i.e., {male →\rightarrow female, female →\rightarrow male} ×\times {pitch, yaw, roll}. We trained regression models to directly output head pose angles in radian, which are roughly in (−0.4​π,0.4​π)(-0.4\pi,0.4\pi).

California Housing [47]. California Housing is a tabular dataset aiming at predicting housing prices from the information of areas. We split the dataset into non-coastal and coastal areas for the source and target domains in accordance with He et al. [24].

More details of the datasets are provided in Sec. C.1.

4.2 Setting

Source model. We used ResNet-26 [23] for SVHN, ResNet-50 for UTKFace and Biwi Kinect, and an MLP for California Housing. We modified the last fully-connected layer to output single scalar values and trained the models with the standard MSE loss on each dataset and task. The details of the training are provided in Appendix C.

Test-time adaptation with SSA (ours). We minimized ℒTTA\mathcal{L}_{\text{TTA}} on the target datasets. We used the outputs of the penultimate layer of the model as features, which had 2048 dimensions. We set the number of dimensions of the feature subspace to K=100K=100 as the default throughout the experiments. More detailed settings are provided in Sec. C.3.

Baseline. Since there are no TTA baselines designed for regression, we compared SSA with TTA methods designed for classification but can be naively modified to regression: Source (no adaptation), BN-adapt [4], Feature restoration (FR) [16], Prototype, Variance minimization (VM), and RSD [6]. In addition, we used the following methods other than TTA as baselines: test-time training (TTT) [53], DANN [21], and Oracle (fine-tuning using labels; performance upper bound). The details of the baseline methods are described in Sec. C.3.

4.3 Results

4.3.1 Number of Dimensions of the Feature Subspace

After the pre-training on the source dataset, we counted the numbers of valid feature dimensions (i.e., having non-zero variances) and dimensions of the feature subspace in which the source features are distributed. The latter value corresponds to the rank of the covariance matrix of the source features in Eq. 5. Tab. 1 shows the result of each source dataset and regression ---TABLE4 FULL---

We evaluated the regression performance in terms of the R2R^{2} score (coefficient of determination), which is widely used in regression tasks (see Appendix B). Tabs. 2 and 3 show the scores for the SVHN-MNIST and California Housing. In the both cases, SSA outperformed the baselines; some of them even underperformed the Source. This is because the baselines were designed for classification tasks and they broke the feature subspaces learned by the source model (see Sec. 4.3.4). On the other hand, RSD [6] is originally designed for regression in UDA but did not work in the California Housing dataset because of numerical instability of SVD performed on every target feature batch. 3.2 Significant-subspace Alignment

In this section, we describe our method, Significant-subspace Alignment (SSA), to tackle the aforementioned problem of naive feature alignment. Fig. 1 shows an overview of SSA. As described in Sec. 3.1, the features of a regression model tend to be distributed in a small subspace of the feature space. Thus, we introduce subspace detection to detect a subspace that is representative and significant to the output and then perform feature alignment in the subspace. Subspace detection is similar to principal component analysis (PCA). Further, in our regression model, a feature 𝐳=gϕ​(𝐱)\mathbf{z}=g_{\phi}(\mathbf{x}) is projected onto a one-dimensional line determined by 𝐰\mathbf{w} of hψh_{\psi} in order to output a scalar value 𝐰⊤​𝐳+b\mathbf{w}^{\top}\mathbf{z}+b. Subspace detection. After the training on the source dataset 𝒮\mathcal{S}, we detect the subspace in which the source features are distributed. Instead of computing the variance of each dimension as Eqs. 1 and 2, we compute the covariance matrix:

We used SVHN and MNIST as the source and target domains, respectively.

UTKFace [59]. UTKFace is a dataset consisting of face images. The task is to predict the age of the person in an input image. For the source model, we trained models on the original UTKFace images. For the target domain, we added corruptions such as noise or blur to the images. The types of corruption were the same as those of ImageNet-C [25]. We applied 13 types of corruption at the highest severity level of the five levels.

Biwi Kinect [18]. Biwi Kinect is a dataset consisting of person images. The task is to predict the head pose of the person in an input image in terms of pitch, yaw, and roll angles. We separately trained models to predict each angle. The source and target domains are the gender of the person in the image. We conducted experiments on six combinations of the source/target gender and task, i.e., {male →\rightarrow female, female →\rightarrow male} ×\times {pitch, yaw, roll}. We trained regression models to directly output head pose angles in radian, which are roughly in (−0.4​π,0.4​π)(-0.4\pi,0.4\pi).

California Housing [47]. California Housing is a tabular dataset aiming at predicting housing prices from the information of areas. We split the dataset into non-coastal and coastal areas for the source and target domains in accordance with He et al. [24].

More details of the datasets are provided in Sec. C.1.

4.2 Setting

Source model. We used ResNet-26 [23] for SVHN, ResNet-50 for UTKFace and Biwi Kinect, and an MLP for California Housing. We modified the last fully-connected layer to output single scalar values and trained the models with the standard MSE loss on each dataset and task. The details of the training are provided in Appendix C.

Test-time adaptation with SSA (ours). We minimized ℒTTA\mathcal{L}_{\text{TTA}} on the target datasets. We used the outputs of the penultimate layer of the model as features, which had 2048 dimensions. We set the number of dimensions of the feature subspace to K=100K=100 as the default throughout the experiments. More detailed settings are provided in Sec. C.3.

Baseline. Since there are no TTA baselines designed for regression, we compared SSA with TTA methods designed for classification but can be naively modified to regression: Source (no adaptation), BN-adapt [4], Feature restoration (FR) [16], Prototype, Variance minimization (VM), and RSD [6]. In addition, we used the following methods other than TTA as baselines: test-time training (TTT) [53], DANN [21], and Oracle (fine-tuning using labels; performance upper bound). The details of the baseline methods are described in Sec. C.3.
